text: One raised reading is not a diagnosis: blood pressure varies markedly, so diagnosis and treatment decisions should not be made on a single occasion, except in a hypertensive crisis

notes: The cuff instruction preserves monitor compatibility and both bladder-to-arm proportions: length 75 to 100% and width 35 to 50%.
text: The cuff should be made for the monitor and sized for the person: bladder length 75 to 100% and width 35 to 50% of the arm circumference

notes: The abnormal-rhythm scope, unreliability of semi-automatic devices and instruction to measure manually by auscultation are retained.
text: In atrial fibrillation and other abnormal rhythms, semi-automatic devices are unreliable, so blood pressure should be measured manually by auscultation

notes: The measurement-quality transition is supported by the rest, repeated readings, cuff and rhythm instructions without prescribing a new measurement technique.
text: Because one number decides so much, it has to be measured well

notes: White-coat hypertension keeps high clinic readings, normal out-of-office readings and prediction of sustained hypertension and cardiovascular disease.
text: White coat hypertension: high clinic blood pressure, normal home or ambulatory readings. It predicts sustained hypertension and cardiovascular disease

notes: Masked hypertension retains normal clinic pressure with raised out-of-office pressure and supported male, smoking and higher-BMI associations.
text: Masked hypertension: normal clinic blood pressure, raised home or ambulatory readings. It is more common in men, smokers and people with a higher body mass index

notes: Every table column preserves both clinic/out-of-office patterns and directs treatment evaluation to out-of-office readings or targets as appropriate.
text: Two patterns a clinic reading can hide. Columns: Pattern | Clinic | Home or ambulatory | Judge treatment by. White coat hypertension | High | Normal | Out-of-office readings. Masked hypertension | Normal | Raised | Out-of-office targets

notes: The linking line accurately frames the clinic-versus-out-of-office contrast shared by white-coat and masked hypertension without adding a management rule.
text: Readings outside the clinic show two patterns a clinic reading hides

notes: Primary hypertension is now described as the most common form rather than a numerical majority, with the uncertain genetic, environmental and vascular-stiffening mechanism retained.
text: Primary (essential) hypertension is the most common form of hypertension: no specific cause that can be treated, thought to come from genes, environment and age-related stiffening of the blood vessels

notes: The risk-factor summary retains the listed ethnic backgrounds and modifiable exposures without turning associations into a diagnostic or prescribing rule.
text: Risk rises with older age, a family history, a Black African, Black Caribbean or South Asian background, a salty diet, being overweight, smoking, too much alcohol and long-term stress

notes: As a transition into causes, the question about why hypertension occurs adds no causal claim beyond the supplied primary-hypertension and risk-factor statements.
text: Once it is confirmed, the next question is why this person has it

notes: The identifiable-cause definition and 5-to-10% frequency of secondary hypertension match; omitting its diagnostic clues does not change an instruction in this definition.
text: Secondary hypertension has an identifiable cause and accounts for 5 to 10% of cases

notes: The screening summary retains every indication branch including specific clinical clues and explicitly points to their full wording rather than silently dropping them.
text: Screen for a secondary cause in resistant, early-onset (before 40), sudden-onset or rapidly worsening, or severe (180/120 mmHg or higher) hypertension; with hypokalaemia on initial testing; with organ damage out of proportion; or with specific clinical clues (listed in the full wording)

notes: About one third remains specific to apparent resistant hypertension, and kidney disease and primary hyperaldosteronism remain the commonest causes.
text: About a third of people with apparent resistant hypertension have a secondary cause, most often kidney disease or primary hyperaldosteronism

notes: The aldosteronism summary restores adult age below 40 and retains consideration strength, both forms of hypokalaemia and the resistant, familial and incidentaloma indications.
text: Primary aldosteronism is the most common endocrine cause of secondary hypertension: screening should be considered in adults under 40, and with spontaneous or thiazide-induced hypokalaemia, resistant hypertension, a family history or an adrenal incidentaloma

notes: The phaeochromocytoma/paraganglioma table row omits sustained hypertension as an alternative to paroxysmal hypertension, narrowing when a student would suspect this cause.
text: Secondary causes: when to suspect each, and the tests the sources name. Columns: Cause | Suspect it with | Tests named. Primary aldosteronism | Adults under 40, hypokalaemia, resistant hypertension, a family history, an adrenal incidentaloma | Plasma aldosterone-renin ratio, after correcting hypokalaemia. Phaeochromocytoma and paraganglioma | Paroxysmal hypertension, headaches, palpitations, sweating | Plasma free or urinary fractionated metanephrines. Cushing syndrome | Truncal obesity, striae, glucose intolerance, repeated infections | Overnight dexamethasone suppression test, 24-hour urine free cortisol. Obstructive sleep apnoea | Snoring, daytime sleepiness, raised body mass index or neck size, non-dipping profile | Epworth or STOP-BANG questionnaire, overnight oxygen saturation. Aortic coarctation | Usually none; radio-femoral delay, lower blood pressure in the legs | MR angiography or CT of the aorta. Renal artery stenosis | Resistant hypertension and/or hypertension starting young, especially in women under 50 | Dedicated imaging (Doppler, CT or MRI) should be considered

notes: A minority and identifiable-cause clues are supported by the 5-to-10% secondary-hypertension statement and its listed screening indications.
text: A minority have a cause that can be found, and some clues point to it

notes: The closing harm statement retains the named organs and all six serious untreated-hypertension outcomes without adding a disease.
text: Untreated, it strains the blood vessels, heart, brain, kidneys and eyes, raising the risk of heart disease, heart attacks, strokes, heart failure, kidney disease and vascular dementia

notes: Premature illness and death faithfully paraphrase morbidity and mortality while preserving worldwide cardiovascular disease and modifiable-risk status.
text: High blood pressure is the leading modifiable risk factor for premature illness and death from cardiovascular disease worldwide

notes: The investigation summary now retains all adults with young-onset hypertension, the consideration strength, clinic plus out-of-office readings and an explicit pointer to the full blood-test list.
text: All adults with young-onset hypertension, investigations to consider: clinic and ambulatory or home blood pressure, ECG, echocardiogram, blood tests (listed in the full wording), fundoscopy, height, weight and waist, urine dipstick

notes: The urinary-infection exclusion and further-investigation instruction remain, and the albumin:creatinine comparison is now explicitly limited to albuminuria.
text: Albuminuria and/or haematuria without a urinary tract infection may indicate renal parenchymal disease or end-organ damage and should be investigated further; for albuminuria, a formal albumin:creatinine ratio is more robust than a dipstick

notes: The fundoscopy instruction retains every severely raised-pressure presentation and now includes slit-lamp examination and pupil dilation if necessary.
text: Fundoscopy should be performed in all patients presenting with severely raised blood pressure, with a slit lamp and pupil dilation if necessary: retinal changes are key to diagnosing malignant hypertension

notes: The linking line introduces damage and the investigations actually named in its support without making those investigations mandatory for every person with hypertension.
text: Next, what raised pressure damages and the investigations the sources name

notes: The dietary components and both systolic reductions, 11.6 mmHg with hypertension and 5.3 mmHg with normal pressure, match the DASH claim.
text: The DASH diet (lean proteins, whole grains, vegetables, fruit, low-fat dairy) lowered systolic pressure by 11.6 mmHg in hypertension and by 5.3 mmHg in normal blood pressure

notes: The lifestyle transition frames the supplied universal lifestyle recommendation and diet, salt, weight and alcohol evidence without specifying a new drug sequence.
text: Bringing it down starts with what the person can change

notes: Drug initiation remains the BIHS position after confirmed sustained out-of-office pressure of at least 135/85 mmHg despite diet and lifestyle advice, regardless of cardiovascular risk.
text: BIHS recommends starting a drug, whatever the cardiovascular risk, after a confirmed diagnosis: a sustained out-of-office blood pressure of 135/85 mmHg or higher despite diet and lifestyle advice

notes: The target retains all-adult scope, six months from starting treatment, below 130/80 or the tolerable achievable alternative, and higher targets for frailty or limited life expectancy.
text: BIHS target for all adults, within 6 months of starting treatment: below 130/80 mmHg, or as low as reasonably achievable without unacceptable side effects; higher targets may be appropriate in frailty and/or limited life expectancy

notes: The same-target instruction preserves the office, 7-day home average and daytime ambulatory average measurement alternatives.
text: BIHS: the target is the same in the clinic, on a 7-day home average and on a daytime ambulatory average

notes: The event reduction remains 10% per 5 mmHg systolic fall down to at least 120 mmHg in people younger than 75.
text: Major cardiovascular events fell in proportion to the fall in systolic pressure: by 10% for each 5 mmHg, down to at least 120 mmHg in people under 75

notes: The transition to drug initiation and targets matches the supplied treatment decisions without inventing a drug, dose or target.
text: Alongside lifestyle, the next decision is when to add a drug and what to aim for

notes: The resistant-hypertension definition now retains daytime ambulatory or home averages, both pressure thresholds, optimal or maximum tolerated doses and both exclusions.
text: Resistant hypertension (BIHS): clinic 140/90 mmHg or higher with average daytime ambulatory or home blood pressure of 135/85 mmHg or higher, despite lifestyle measures and at least 3 drugs at optimal or maximum tolerated doses, with non-adherence and secondary causes excluded

notes: Pseudo-resistance is now described through its common measurement and adherence causes, without adding an unsupported assertion about its overall prevalence.
text: Pseudo-resistant hypertension commonly results from inaccurate measurement (an inaccurate device or wrong-sized cuff, the white-coat phenomenon, or marked brachial artery calcification); non-adherence is also a frequent cause

notes: Around 50% non-adherence remains attached to apparent resistant hypertension and to objective blood or urine drug measurements.
text: Objective tests of drugs in blood or urine show non-adherence in around 50% of people with apparent resistant hypertension

notes: The fourth-line instruction retains persistently raised pressure despite optimal triple therapy and correctly attributes the spironolactone result to PATHWAY-2.
text: If blood pressure stays raised on optimal triple therapy, a fourth-line drug should be added; the PATHWAY-2 trial found spironolactone lowered it most

notes: The spironolactone summary preserves resistant-hypertension scope, fourth-line should strength, 12.5 to 25 mg daily, renal and potassium conditions and response-dependent increase to 50 mg.
text: In resistant hypertension, spironolactone should be used as the fourth-line drug of choice: started at 12.5 to 25 mg once daily (if eGFR is above 30 and potassium below 4.5 mmol/L), and can be increased to 50 mg depending on clinical response

notes: Checking diagnosis, pseudo-resistance, adherence and optimal triple therapy before adding treatment is a supported framing of the supplied resistant-hypertension steps.
text: If pressure stays above target on treatment, the basics are checked before more is added

notes: The above-180/120 mmHg threshold still triggers urgent assessment, with the same urgency as the claim.
text: Blood pressure above 180/120 mmHg needs an urgent assessment

notes: The emergency definition retains sustained pressure over hours and life-threatening damage, with its four named examples drawn from the supporting list.
text: Hypertensive emergency: raised blood pressure that, if sustained over hours, may lead to life-threatening organ damage, as in pulmonary oedema, encephalopathy, aortic dissection or intracerebral haemorrhage

notes: The malignant-hypertension definition keeps the typical diastolic threshold of at least 120 mmHg and concurrent bilateral grade 3 or grade 4 retinal disease.
text: Malignant hypertension: typically diastolic 120 mmHg or higher, with bilateral grade 3 or grade 4 hypertensive retinopathy

notes: The absence of life-threatening damage remains the condition for days-to-weeks reduction with oral rather than intravenous treatment.
text: Severe hypertension without life-threatening damage: lowered over days to weeks rather than hours, by mouth rather than intravenously

notes: The first-6-to-24-hour pressure limits and aortic exception match, but the summary omits the requirement for immediate attention, potentially allowing assessment or management to be delayed.
text: Hypertensive emergency, first 6 to 24 hours: a controlled but only partial reduction in mean arterial pressure, of no more than 20 to 25%, aiming to keep diastolic blood pressure above 100 mmHg except in acute aortic syndromes

notes: The low-pressure perfusion warning stays scoped to chronic hypertension with upward-shifted autoregulation, rather than claiming normalisation is harmless.
text: In chronic hypertension autoregulation is reset higher, so lowering blood pressure to low values can compromise blood flow to vital organs

notes: Both table paths now preserve slow oral treatment without life-threatening damage and immediate emergency attention with most-cases parallel assessment, the MAP limit and diastolic exception.

How | Oral rather than intravenous therapy | Immediate attention; in most cases management begins in parallel with assessment

notes: The urgency transition is supported by the severe-reading assessment and emergency claims and does not itself impose rapid lowering on uncomplicated severe hypertension.
text: Very high readings change how fast everything happens

notes: Adult age below 40 at diagnosis, specialist review and both purposes of that review are retained without strengthening the recommendation.
text: Adults diagnosed under 40 (young-onset hypertension) are recommended for review by a hypertension specialist, to exclude secondary causes and optimise treatment

notes: The temporary non-RAAS drug preference retains newly diagnosed patients awaiting specialist review, the three eligibility triggers and amlodipine as an example.
text: Newly diagnosed and awaiting a specialist, if under 40, post-partum or a secondary cause is suspected: a drug that leaves the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system alone, such as amlodipine, is preferred for now

notes: The pregnancy summary restores young-onset and childbearing-potential scope, contraception discussion and where-appropriate harm advice, while pointing to the full pregnancy-drug wording.
text: Young-onset hypertension, women of childbearing potential: discuss plans for future pregnancy and contraception use and, where appropriate, the potential harmful effects of ACE inhibitors and angiotensin II receptor antagonists in pregnancy; drugs routinely used in pregnancy are named in the full wording

notes: The postural-hypotension instruction now retains symptoms as an independent trigger alongside all five risk groups and the standing treatment target.
text: Postural hypotension should be checked for in people with frailty, aged over 80, with multi-morbidity, type 2 diabetes or Parkinson's disease, or with symptoms; if present, treat to a standing target

notes: The adjustment transition adds no new patient category or treatment and is supported by the specialist, pregnancy and postural-hypotension claims.
text: Some people need the plan adjusted

notes: The guess-first scenario now excludes hypertensive crisis and its explanation retains that exception and the instruction for ambulatory or home confirmation.
text: A clinic blood pressure reading is raised and there is no hypertensive crisis. What should come next? Answer: Confirm it with home or ambulatory readings. Blood pressure varies markedly within a person, so a diagnosis should not be made on a single occasion, except in a hypertensive crisis: it should be confirmed by ambulatory or home monitoring.

notes: The explain-later question explicitly excludes hypertensive crisis and retains variability, out-of-office confirmation and the two clinic-versus-home patterns.
text: Explain why, outside a hypertensive crisis, one raised clinic reading is not enough to diagnose hypertension, and what is done instead. A good answer covers: Blood pressure varies markedly within a person; A hypertensive crisis is the exception; The diagnosis should be confirmed by ambulatory or home monitoring; Clinic and home can disagree: white coat and masked hypertension.

notes: The big idea fixes diagnostic and drug-starting conditions but its emergency-treatment instruction still omits the diastolic floor above 100 mmHg and the acute-aortic-syndrome exception.
text: High blood pressure is common, usually silent, and the leading modifiable risk factor for premature illness and death from cardiovascular disease. Outside a hypertensive crisis, one raised reading is not a diagnosis: it is confirmed with home or ambulatory readings. Then: look for a cause where the clues point to one, know what untreated pressure damages, and bring it down, with lifestyle interventions for everyone and, in the BIHS position, a drug once out-of-office blood pressure stays at 135/85 mmHg or higher despite diet and lifestyle advice. A hypertensive emergency needs immediate attention, with only a partial reduction at first.

notes: The closing diagnostic line retains the two measurement settings and thresholds and explicitly limits the single-occasion prohibition to cases outside hypertensive crisis.
text: A reading counts as high at 140/90 taken by a healthcare professional or 135/85 at home. Outside a hypertensive crisis, a diagnosis is not made on a single occasion: it is confirmed by ambulatory or home monitoring.

notes: The closing line retains early-onset and resistant screening triggers with a pointer to other clues, universal hypertensive lifestyle advice and the adult target with intolerance and frailty alternatives.
text: Screen for a secondary cause when hypertension starts before 40, is resistant, or comes with hypokalaemia or other clues. Lifestyle interventions are for everyone with hypertension. The BIHS target for adults is below 130/80 mmHg, or as low as reasonably achievable without unacceptable side effects, with higher targets where appropriate in frailty or limited life expectancy.

notes: The emergency recap now preserves above-180/120 urgency, the 6-to-24-hour partial MAP limit, the diastolic floor and aortic exception alongside the supported perfusion warning.
text: Blood pressure above 180/120 mmHg needs an urgent assessment. In a hypertensive emergency the first reduction is controlled and only partial (mean arterial pressure by no more than 20 to 25% in 6 to 24 hours, keeping diastolic above 100 mmHg except in acute aortic syndromes), because lowering blood pressure to low values can compromise blood flow to vital organs.
